title: GIM AI Assistants Registry | AI Ops OS
description:
One record per client AI Operations Assistant. Each subtask is one assistant: J.A.R.V.I.S. (Juvibolt), I.V.Y. (InVogue Cleans), N.E.O. (NoirLab), R.I.V.A. (RiseWise), R.O.C.K.Y. (We Rock the Spectrum), L.I.L.O. (Little Treasures), plus G.I.A. (Gianna), GIM's own AI Chief of Staff. Each client subtask also shows in its client's list.

Registry doc (one page per assistant): https://app.clickup.com/9016642965/docs/8cpy3cn-20196

THESE ARE A GUIDE, NOT A BUILD ORDER
They don't all have to be built now. Every record is a draft pulled on 11 Nov 2026 from GIM's ClickUp, Grace In Motion Slack and GIM notes, plus the GIM Client AI Assistants Master Reference. The details still need to be verified. RA and Radz hold a call with the assigned OM for each account BEFORE creating that client's AI Assistant MVP. If and when each MVP is built is decided on that call.

WHAT THE REGISTRY TRACKS (per assistant)
- Official name, meaning, role, personality
- OM to verify with, and verification status (pending, or verified with date)
- Implementation phase: 1 Operations Foundation, 2 AI-Assisted Operations, 3 Operational Automation, 4 AI-Enabled Business Management
- Connected tools and the access the assistant needs
- Automation coverage, with four labels: Human-owned, AI-assisted, Eligible for automation, Automated and validated
- Which workflows still need a human (approvals and escalations)

RULES
- Nothing is labelled "Automated and validated" unless it was built and tested. Note where the test is logged.
- One record per assistant. No second version of the same identity anywhere else; link to this registry instead.
- No passwords, keys, tokens or pay rates in the registry or the tasks.
- Each client's data stays in its own record. Nothing from one client goes into another client's channels or docs.

WHEN A RECORD IS VERIFIED
1. Update its page in the registry doc: change "Verification: Pending OM call" to "Verified with (OM), (date)", and fix anything the OM corrected.
2. Swap the tag om-verification-pending for om-verified on the subtask.
3. If the OM agrees to build now, create the MVP build task(s) in the client's list and link them to the subtask.

This registry is the start of GIM's standard AI Ops OS for every new client.

title: Dr. Yasmin x Divine
description:
Brief for BJ — Dr. Yasmin Davidds Leadership Institute (DYDLI): Proposal
From: Divine Grace Origines Date issued: 30 July 2026 Due back to Divine: ASAP — high priority Priority: High. This is a live prospect who has asked for a proposal so she can decide whether to move forward. She is comparing us against other fractional COO candidates.
Note on this brief: everything below is my own material — the discovery call transcript, the prospect's written messages, and the emails I already sent her. Nothing here is external research or third-party analysis. Work only from what is in this document. If you need a fact we don't have, that is a signal to flag it to me, not to fill the gap.
1. The situation
Dr. Yasmin Davidds is the Founder and CEO of the Dr. Yasmin Davidds Leadership Institute (DYDLI), a founder-led leadership development company. She reached out on Upwork, we had a full discovery call on 30 July 2026, and she has since sent a detailed written message asking for a formal proposal.
This is not a competition submission like the Little Treasures brief — this is a real proposal for a real prospective client. She is genuinely evaluating whether to hire us, alongside other candidates, and has told me pricing needs to be competitive and reasonable.
I have already sent her one written reply (before the discovery call, in response to her initial outreach) that committed to a specific engagement shape: a four-phase structure, a 12–16 week hands-on engagement, and an initial phase requiring approximately 20–30 hours per week. The new proposal must be consistent with that reply, not contradict it. That reply is reproduced in full in Section 4 below — treat it as a prior commitment, not a first draft.
She has since asked for something much more detailed and structured than that initial reply. Her request (reproduced in Section 5) is essentially a full proposal outline in her own words. Follow her requested structure closely — she told us exactly what she wants to see.
2. What you are producing
Three things, because she asked for three things.
Deliverable 1 — The main proposal (client-facing)
The phased operational diagnostic and implementation proposal, built around the four phases I already committed to, broken out with objectives, activities, deliverables, timeline, hours, cost, and everything else she listed in Section 5 below. Includes the 30-60-90 day plan she asked for as the output of the diagnostic phase.
Deliverable 2 — The Virtual Executive Assistant workstream (client-facing, can be part of the same document or a clearly separated section/appendix — your call on formatting, but content must be complete)
She wants this treated as a separate, urgent, optional workstream — not gated behind the full diagnostic. See Section 5 for exactly what she asked for here.
Deliverable 3 — The Los Angeles Program Manager recruitment workstream (client-facing, same treatment as Deliverable 2)
Also urgent, also separate. See Section 5.
Deliverable 4 — Internal appendix (not sent to Dr. Yasmin)
A short internal document for me: the discovery question set I would use in the kickoff call, and a list of everything in this brief that is a genuine open question or missing input, so I can chase it down before or during the diagnostic. See Section 9.
Format: Markdown, so I can edit quickly. I will handle final formatting/branding before sending anything to her.
3. Confirmed facts about DYDLI
Everything in this section is directly confirmed either in her written overview letter, her Upwork message, or the call transcript. Treat all of it as usable, factual material.
Company: Dr. Yasmin Davidds Leadership Institute. Founder-led leadership development company. Designs and delivers customised leadership development programs for colleges, corporations, foundations, and other institutional clients.
Business model: DYDLI is paid by the institution (the college, corporation, or foundation), not by individual participants. Programs are typically turnkey, high-touch, multi-month engagements priced between $150,000 and $250,000 per program, paid across multiple instalments over the year. There is no consumer-facing sales funnel, no advertising, and no lead generation in the traditional sense — new business comes from referral and word of mouth between institutional decision-makers (e.g., one college president referring another).
Revenue: Approximately $800,000–$850,000 in current annual revenue (her written overview states ~$850,000; she also referenced ~$800,000 for "last year" on the call). Treat this as one range, not two separate numbers — don't force false precision. She has stated an ambition to reach approximately $2 million next year if she continues landing large institutional contracts, and has one program in active negotiation for a new client type (a "young men of color" college program, approximately $250,000, targeted for delivery in February 2027 — her first time delivering that specific program design, still in the negotiation/design stage as of the call).
12-month goal: She stated a goal of growing from her current program count to roughly 9–10 programs running concurrently within 12 months — a significant multiple of current volume. Note a discrepancy to flag, don't silently resolve it: her website lists (and she confirmed) approximately five programs, but on the call she referenced growing "from three programs" toward that 9–10 target. Use a phrase like "her current handful of active programs" rather than picking one number — this is a good discovery/appendix item, not something to smooth over in the client-facing proposal.
Programs: Approximately five programs listed on her website (she confirmed this is roughly accurate), run at different times of year, some virtual and some in-person. Each program follows a detailed internal blueprint — built in Excel — of roughly 160 sequential steps (dependencies, application steps, scheduling, etc.). Programs overlap significantly in structure but are not identical: she described roughly four distinct programs having as many as seven different variations depending on the client.
Team (as of the 30 July call): Dr. Yasmin (Founder/CEO), one Managing Director who oversees Program Managers and manages institutional relationships, and one Program Manager who was hired approximately two weeks before the call and is still being trained. Her written overview (dated 19 July, ahead of the call) describes a four-person team "in process of replacing the 4th person" — consistent with the newer hire referenced on the call. She is actively hiring: two more Program Managers within the next month, one of which must be based in Los Angeles for in-person work at a college campus (this is the recruitment workstream in Deliverable 3). She also intends to hire a Virtual Executive Assistant as soon as possible (Deliverable 2). Competitive context: she mentioned on the call that she has a separate appointment scheduled with Athena, a virtual executive assistant company, to hear their offering — meaning she is actively evaluating at least one other option for the EA role alongside ours. Write the EA workstream to stand on its own strengths (speed to start, integration with an operations relationship she already has) rather than referencing or comparing against Athena directly.
Current tools: Zoom (for virtual program delivery), Google Workspace (Google Docs, Google Drive for live/current documents), Dropbox (archived/inactive program materials), Microsoft Outlook (email), Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, used offline then uploaded to Google as needed), ChatGPT (heavy day-to-day use across the team — there is an internal Teams chat channel and a stated "use AI first" culture). There is no CRM and no central project management platform in place today.
Confirmed operational pain points (her own words, from the call and the letter):
A recurring pattern of missed deadlines, which she explicitly does not want to normalise as "just how it is."
Documents are hard to find in Google Drive because of inconsistent, ad hoc file naming (her own example: a graduate marketing asset was named "SM" for "social media" with no reference to "graduate," and the team lost a day recreating it before finding the original).
The Managing Director is currently training the new Program Manager while also running her own programs, and Dr. Yasmin has observed the training quality suffering as a result.
No clarity on what a new Program Manager should already know versus what needs to be trained — she gave a concrete example (calendar invites) of a skill she assumed was baseline but ended up being taught.
No visibility into team capacity. She does not know whether one person can run one program, or more than one, and is currently hiring "by guessing."
Her Managing Director does not consistently apply lessons learned on one program to the other programs — Dr. Yasmin described this as a gap in "systems thinking" and said she has to repeatedly remind the team that changes should be considered across all programs, not just the one in front of them.
She estimated that roughly half of a typical day is spent cleaning up mistakes that trace back to the lack of sustainable systems (her own estimate — not a measured figure, so it should be framed as her characterisation, not a stated metric).
She is the company's sole salesperson and primary business developer, in addition to being lead facilitator, principal subject-matter expert, and final decision-maker/quality-control authority. Every hour she spends on operational firefighting is time she is not spending on business development, relationship-building with college presidents, or programme design — and she named this directly as a growth constraint (she wants to attend more events and build more institutional relationships but currently doesn't trust the operations to handle the added volume).
She has previously tried to step back from day-to-day operations and had to step back in because deliverables were missed or details fell through the cracks when she did.
She is aware her own role as lead facilitator/"talent" for the core transformation methodology is not something operational systems can replace or fully delegate — she was explicit that she is "the visionary" and "the talent," and that this part of the business stays with her.
Technology decision in progress (handle carefully — see Section 6): Her outside technology consultant has recommended migrating from Google Workspace to Microsoft 365/SharePoint, primarily for identity/security consolidation (all DYDLI email already runs on Microsoft 365/Outlook) and because DYDLI's actual work product — Word, Excel, PowerPoint documents, matching what colleges and institutional partners use — is Microsoft-native. In my initial reply to her (before the discovery call) I recommended staying on Google Drive because migration is costly and the underlying problem (poor file naming/findability) isn't solved by a platform switch alone. She subsequently ran both recommendations through ChatGPT (which she has fed a lot of company context over time) and it sided with her consultant's Microsoft 365 recommendation. My most recent written reply to her (Section 4) walked that back appropriately — I said I would not recommend either platform without a proper assessment of current workflows, and that I've previously implemented Microsoft/SharePoint environments for a client generating approximately $144 million annually, so this is not a capability gap on our side.
Security/compliance note: her tech consultant has raised concerns about uploading confidential company documents to ChatGPT. Dr. Yasmin's position on the call was that the business already does this regularly and considers it necessary, but she is open to finding "a middle ground" between usability and protection. This is a live tension between her technology consultant and her own current practice — flag it as a discovery/governance item, don't resolve it in the proposal.
Her own stated frameworks — these are hers, not ours. Use them, and credit them as things she already believes, because it shows we listened:
"If you can Google it, we shouldn't be training on it" — her rule that internal training time should be reserved for DYDLI-specific knowledge, not general skills a hire should already have.
Her SOP quality bar: an SOP is working if someone with no prior context (she used the phrase "a grade 3 student") could follow it without getting stuck.
4. My prior written reply — the engagement shape already on record
I sent Dr. Yasmin this reply before our discovery call, in response to her initial outreach message. The four-phase structure and the 12–16 week estimate still hold and should not be silently changed. The 20–30 hours/week figure does NOT hold — see the note below before you write the hours/timeline sections.
UPDATE — hours estimate is being revised upward. Use 40–50 hours/week, not 20–30.
The 20–30 hrs/week figure below was my estimate before the discovery call, made without knowing the actual state of her systems. The call confirmed there is currently no CRM and no central project management platform in place at all — not an underused one, not a fragmented one, literally nothing. That's a materially bigger build than the estimate assumed, so the real number is closer to 40–50 hours per week for the hands-on phases.
Do not just swap the number silently. Write one or two sentences into the proposal (probably in the phase breakdown or right where hours are introduced) that explicitly ties the revision to that finding — something like: the initial estimate was made before the discovery call, and now that we've confirmed there is no existing CRM or project management system to build from, the scope is larger than first estimated. This keeps me consistent and credible rather than looking like I lowballed to win the deal and inflated it after.
I don't yet have the split between my personal hours and my team's hours within that 40–50, so don't attempt a blended rate calculation — just present the revised total hours honestly, keep cost cells as placeholders per Section 7, and I'll finalize the breakdown separately.
Hi Dr. Yasmin,
Thank you for taking the time to provide such a detailed overview. Based on what you shared, this engagement strongly aligns with the work I do as a Fractional COO — helping founder-led companies reduce operational dependence on the CEO by building clear systems, accountability, and decision-making infrastructure that the team can consistently execute.
My initial assessment is that the primary bottleneck is not simply a lack of documentation. It is that operational knowledge, decision-making authority, prioritization, and quality control still ultimately lead back to the CEO.
The goal would be to build a centralized operating system that allows the team to execute independently while giving the CEO appropriate visibility and control without requiring her daily involvement.
Where I would begin
I would begin with a structured operational diagnostic covering: the full client and program delivery lifecycle; current team roles, ownership, and decision-making authority; existing systems, spreadsheets, SOPs, and reporting tools; recurring execution failures, missed handoffs, and communication gaps; CEO approval points and escalation patterns; hiring, onboarding, finance, reporting, and AI-use workflows; business continuity risks tied to individual team members.
Following the diagnostic, I would develop a customised 30-60-90 Day Business and Operations Plan that would serve as the implementation blueprint for the engagement, outlining: the highest-priority operational risks and bottlenecks; what needs to be stabilized, built, or improved; specific deliverables and implementation milestones; ownership and accountability across the team; success metrics and expected outcomes; the sequence in which systems should be implemented; which responsibilities can be gradually transitioned away from the CEO.
The plan would not simply be a list of recommendations. It would guide the hands-on implementation, testing, and team adoption process.
What I would personally build and implement
I would personally lead the operational architecture and implementation, including: a centralised operations and program management system; reusable client and program delivery templates; clear ownership, decision rights, and escalation protocols; hiring and onboarding workflows that reduce CEO involvement to one defined approval point; SOP and training standards with quality-control checkpoints; management dashboards, reporting rhythms, and accountability systems; finance-related approval and visibility workflows; practical AI governance protocols; team training, system testing, implementation, and ownership transfer.
Your existing team would be involved in validating current workflows, identifying exceptions, testing the new systems, and eventually taking ownership of them. However, they would not be expected to independently design and implement the entire operational infrastructure.
I would remain accountable for the overall structure, implementation, and adoption. Where appropriate, my operations team can also support system configuration, documentation, migration, and quality assurance under my direction.
How I would reduce daily dependence on the CEO
I would not recommend removing the CEO from operations all at once. Instead, we would gradually replace daily involvement with: defined approval thresholds; a decision-rights matrix; clear escalation criteria; weekly executive reporting; program health and risk indicators; quality-control gates before client-facing delivery; structured leadership meetings focused on exceptions, risks, and decisions rather than task-level updates.
This allows the CEO to step back without losing visibility or discovering problems only after a deadline or client commitment has been missed.
Recommended engagement structure
I would likely structure the engagement in four phases:
Diagnostic and Stabilization — review the current operating environment, identify immediate risks, and address urgent execution gaps.
30-60-90 Day Planning and System Design — develop the implementation blueprint and design the centralised workflows, templates, dashboards, decision rights, and accountability structures.
Implementation and Team Adoption — build and configure the systems, test them under real operating conditions, refine the workflows, and train the team.
Transition and Optimization — transfer ownership, monitor performance, and confirm that the company is no longer dependent on one person holding the operational knowledge.
Based on the scope described, I would initially estimate a hands-on engagement of approximately 12–16 weeks, followed by a lighter optimisation or ongoing Fractional COO support period.
The initial diagnostic and implementation phase would likely require approximately 20–30 hours per week, depending on the condition of the existing systems, the number of active programs, the complexity of the workflows, and the level of hands-on implementation required.
[She then went on to list what she'd need to review to firm this up, and proposed a discovery call — which we then had.]
5. Her exact request — this is the required outline
This is what she sent after the discovery call. Follow this structure directly — it is not a suggestion, it's what she asked to see.
For the phased proposal, each phase must include:
The specific objectives and scope
The activities to be completed
The deliverables DYDLI will receive
The anticipated timeline
The estimated hours
The proposed cost
Whether hourly, fixed-price, or retainer
What I would personally perform
What members of my team would perform
The assumptions or circumstances that could affect the price
The measurable outcomes that would indicate the phase was successfully completed
For the initial diagnostic phase specifically, the final deliverable must also include a prioritised 30-60-90 day implementation plan identifying:
What needs to be stabilised immediately
What systems need to be built or improved
Recommended role and responsibility changes
Recommended hiring or contractor needs
Which responsibilities should remain internal to DYDLI
Which responsibilities could appropriately be supported by our team
Implementation priorities, estimated hours, projected costs, and success measures
She also asked for a preliminary range for the broader implementation engagement (i.e., roughly what the whole thing costs, phase 1 through phase 4), understanding that the final scope and budget may change after the diagnostic.
Virtual Executive Assistant workstream — separate, urgent, not gated on the diagnostic. Must cover:
How our Virtual EA contracting process works
Information on any qualified candidates currently available through our organisation
Their experience and areas of expertise
Proposed responsibilities
Working hours and Pacific Time availability
Hourly or monthly rate
Whether the individual would be dedicated to DYDLI or shared across clients
Who would manage and evaluate their performance
Any agency, management, placement, or conversion fees
What would happen if DYDLI later wished to hire the individual directly
Los Angeles Program Manager recruitment workstream — separate, urgent. This person will be a direct DYDLI employee, full-time, on-site, not a contractor supplied by us on an ongoing basis. We are recruiting-only for this role. Must cover:
Refining the role scorecard and job description
Developing the recruitment strategy
Sourcing candidates
Conducting initial screening
Supporting structured interviews
Coordinating reference checks
Presenting qualified finalists
Proposed process, timeline, deliverables, fee structure, and any placement guarantee
Make explicit that DYDLI is the employer of record and retains final authority over candidate selection, compensation, classification, and employment terms
Her seven direct questions (from her original overview message) — make sure all seven are visibly and directly answered somewhere in the proposal, not just implied:
Where I would begin
What I believe DYDLI's most significant operational bottleneck is
Whether this type of engagement aligns with my experience and working style
What I would personally build and implement versus what I would assign to her existing team
How I would reduce the team's daily dependence on the CEO without allowing deliverables to fall through the cracks
The approximate timeline and weekly commitment I would recommend
How I would structure an initial diagnostic and implementation engagement
6. Technology position — handle with care
Do not recommend Google Drive, and do not recommend SharePoint/Microsoft 365, as a settled decision in this proposal. Both my own prior stance and Dr. Yasmin's tech consultant's stance are on record, and I have already told her (in a message after the ChatGPT exchange) that I wouldn't recommend either platform without a proper assessment first, and that I have direct experience building on Microsoft/SharePoint for a company generating roughly $144 million annually — so this is not a competency gap, it's a sequencing discipline. Stay consistent with that position.
Frame the platform decision as one of the outputs of the diagnostic phase, decided against clear criteria (what problem it solves, cost/effort of migration, how the team actually works today, security and identity requirements, alignment with institutional partners' formats, who owns and maintains it).
Explicitly note that her existing technology consultant is a stakeholder to coordinate with during discovery, not a rival recommendation to overrule. She has already said she wants communication between "the tech people building that out" and us.
Where the proposal needs to refer to systems before that decision is made, use function, not platform name: "the central program and project management system," "the document and knowledge repository," "the email and calendar platform."
It is fine to note the underlying problem she actually described (poor file naming and findability) is a governance/naming-convention problem that exists independent of which platform she picks — that's a legitimate diagnostic finding, not a platform recommendation.
AI governance is something she explicitly asked for in her own overview letter ("AI use, access, quality control, confidentiality, and decision-making are governed through practical AI governance standards and documented protocols"). Treat this as a named deliverable in the relevant phase — not an afterthought. Acknowledge the team's existing heavy ChatGPT use and the "use AI first" culture as the starting point, and note the tension between her tech consultant's confidentiality concerns and her own current practice as something the governance protocol needs to resolve, not something this proposal resolves unilaterally.
7. Hard rules — do not break these
Do not invent anything. Specifically, do not invent or imply:
named EA candidates, their résumés, experience, or availability — we don't have specific people to name in this draft; write the contracting process fully, and leave the "currently available candidates" section as something I will insert once I check with my team (see Section 9)
specific EA or Program Manager recruitment pricing, hourly rates, monthly rates, placement fees, or guarantee terms — I have not given you numbers for these; leave them as clearly marked inputs for me to fill in, structured exactly where the number would go
specific phase costs in dollars — you can and should build hour ranges and phase timelines, anchored to the 12–16 week / 20–30 hours-per-week figures I already gave her in writing (Section 4). Do not convert hours into dollar costs — I have not given you a rate. Leave cost cells clearly marked for me to complete once I confirm the rate with you.
team members, team size, or roles at DYDLI beyond what is confirmed in Section 3
revenue, program counts, or client numbers beyond what is confirmed in Section 3 — and don't force false precision where I've given you a range
past outcomes, percentages, or measurable results for DYDLI — none exist yet
market statistics or industry benchmarks for leadership development or higher-education institutional sales
quotes from Dr. Yasmin beyond what is in this brief
If you find yourself needing a fact we don't have, flag it as a discovery item or leave it as a placeholder — do not fill the gap with something plausible.
Never present an assumption as a fact. Where the proposal makes an assumption (e.g., about team capacity, about which workflows are highest-priority), label it as something the diagnostic will confirm or correct.
Do not guarantee outcomes. We can describe what the engagement is designed to produce; we cannot promise specific results for DYDLI.
Things only I can supply — write around them

Do not write Because Write instead
Specific hourly rate or my day rate I haven't given you one yet Structure the cost line clearly (e.g., "Estimated hours: X–Y hrs/week · Proposed cost:  [rate to be confirmed] ") so I can drop the number straight in
EA hourly/monthly rate, placement/conversion fees Not yet set for this brief Same treatment — structured placeholder, not a guess
Program Manager recruitment fee structure or placement guarantee terms Not yet set for this brief Same treatment
Named EA candidates and their backgrounds We don't have specific people confirmed for this draft Describe the contracting/vetting process in full; note current candidate availability as something I'll confirm before this goes out
Case study numbers from unrelated past clients (e.g., the e-commerce coaching business, the 332.6% or 2.2x figures) Different business model — consumer coaching with paid ads and IG DM funnels, nothing like DYDLI's institutional B2B model. Repeating those specifics here risks implying we'd bring the same playbook (ad funnels, DM setters) to an institutional leadership business, which would be wrong and could read as generic/copy-pasted If a case study reference is useful at all, keep it to one line noting relevant experience is available on request — do not repeat funnel/DM-setter mechanics or specific growth percentages from that business
A confident claim about what her tech consultant "should" do Not our call to make unilaterally Frame platform decisions as a joint, criteria-based decision made during diagnostic, in coordination with her existing consultant
Definitive statements about data privacy, confidentiality, or compliance obligations for AI use with institutional/education clients We're not positioned to make legal claims State that AI governance protocols would be developed collaboratively and, where needed, validated against her institutional clients' own data and confidentiality requirements
8. Voice and writing style
Write as me: warm, direct, hands-on, confident without being salesy, practical. This is a real proposal to a real prospect who has been very engaged and complimentary on the call — match that warmth, but keep the substance doing the work, not the tone.
US English throughout (not Australian — different client, different brief).
It should not sound like: a templated agency pitch deck, a generic consulting proposal, an over-promised sales page, or a copy-paste of the Little Treasures document with names swapped. This client explicitly told us she wants specificity, phased accountability, and clear cost logic — give her that, not enthusiasm.

Grounding rule: every recommendation should trace back to something she actually told us — a named pain point, a named goal, or one of her seven questions. If a sentence doesn't trace back to something in Section 3 or Section 5, cut it.
Avoid the same category of filler language as always: unlock potential, leverage synergies, seamless execution, cutting-edge, revolutionise, streamline operations (without explaining the actual mechanism), operational excellence, robust, holistic, empower, game-changing, scalable solutions, best-in-class. If a sentence needs one of these, explain the mechanism instead.
Tables are appropriate here — this is a proposal, not the Little Treasures roadmap, and she explicitly asked for structured, itemised information (objectives, activities, deliverables, timeline, hours, cost, per phase). Use tables where they make the phase breakdowns easier to scan. Don't over-format everything into tables where prose reads better — the reasoning behind each phase, the tie-back to her pain points, and the framing sections should read as prose.

Do not make her feel criticised. She has been candid and vulnerable about what isn't working (missed deadlines, training quality, her own time being consumed by cleanup). Frame every gap as the natural result of a company that has grown its client roster faster than its internal infrastructure — not as a leadership failure on her part.
9. Deliverable 4 — Internal appendix (not sent to Dr. Yasmin)
A short internal working document. Two parts:
Discovery question set for the kickoff call, grouped by area (program delivery lifecycle, team roles and capacity, current systems and tools, hiring and onboarding, finance/approvals, AI use and governance, technology/platform decision). Pull from the gaps identified in Section 3 and the diagnostic scope already committed to in Section 4. Aim for 30–50 questions, ordered so they could be worked through in a single structured call.
Open items list for me — everything in this brief flagged in Section 7 as "only I can supply" (rate, EA candidate info, recruitment fee structure, placement guarantee terms), listed together in one place so I can address them quickly before this goes out to her.
2–3 pages. Flexible length.
10. Checklist before you send it back to me
[ ] All four phases from Section 4 are present and consistent with what I already told her — no silent changes to the phase names or the 12–16 week estimate
[ ] Hours estimate updated to 40–50 hrs/week (not the old 20–30) with a sentence explaining why, per the note in Section 4
[ ] Every phase includes all eleven elements she asked for in Section 5 (objectives/scope, activities, deliverables, timeline, hours, cost, arrangement type, what I do, what my team does, assumptions, success measures)
[ ] The 30-60-90 day plan is present as the diagnostic phase's final deliverable, with all seven elements she asked for
[ ] A preliminary range for the full engagement is included, clearly marked as subject to change after diagnostic
[ ] EA workstream present, structured as its own section, all nine elements she asked for addressed or clearly placeholdered
[ ] LA Program Manager recruitment workstream present, structured as its own section, all elements addressed, employer-of-record language included
[ ] All seven of her direct questions are visibly and separately answerable by reading the document
[ ] No dollar figures invented — every cost cell is either a real number I gave you or a clearly marked placeholder
[ ] No named EA candidates invented
[ ] Nothing from the unrelated coaching-business case study repeated in mechanic or number
[ ] Platform decision (Google vs. Microsoft/SharePoint) is not settled in this document — framed as a diagnostic-phase, criteria-based decision made in coordination with her existing tech consultant
[ ] AI governance appears as a named deliverable, not an afterthought
[ ] Every recommendation traces to something she actually said (Section 3 or Section 5)
[ ] She would not feel criticised reading any part of it
[ ] US English throughout
[ ] No banned filler phrases
[ ] Internal appendix delivered as a separate file, not attached to the client-facing proposal
11. If something is unclear
Come to me before you start writing, not after the draft — this one's urgent, so the faster you flag a gap, the faster I can close it. If something in this brief seems thin, contradictory, or like it needs a number only I have, flag it immediately rather than guessing.

title: Little Treasures Company: Six-Month Operational Roadmap
description:
Note on this brief: everything below is my own material — Zoe's job post and assignment, my application to her, my answers to her questions, and my operational principles. Nothing here is external research or third-party analysis. Work only from what is in this document.
1. The situation
I have been shortlisted as one of the final three candidates for a long-term Founding Operations and AI Architect role with Zoe Horner, founder of Little Treasures Therapy, a paediatric Occupational Therapy practice based in Perth, Western Australia.

Zoe wants the final stage to focus on how I think, plan and build rather than another interview. She has asked me to prepare a detailed but concise Six-Month Operational Roadmap.

She asked me to imagine I had already accepted the role and had been working with her for six months, and to describe exactly what I would have achieved by that point. She wants a practical and detailed plan rather than broad ideas.

She has offered to pay for up to two hours of my time for the exercise. Pricing and my hourly rate do not appear anywhere in the document.

I replied to her: "Of course! I'll be sending a case study as well." So the roadmap may briefly reference that a supporting case study is included separately — but must not repeat the case study inside it.
2. What Zoe wants to understand
She wants to see:
what I would investigate first
how I would turn her ideas into operational execution
what systems I would build
what I would prioritise
why I would prioritise those areas
what deliverables would exist after six months
how success would be measured
how I would reduce founder dependency
how I would ensure the business does not become dependent on me
how I would prepare the company for future growth
The document must demonstrate real operational judgement, not just familiarity with software.
3. About Zoe and Little Treasures
The business and the vision
Little Treasures Therapy is a paediatric Occupational Therapy practice in Perth, Western Australia.
Zoe's long-term vision is to transform Little Treasures from a traditional therapy business into an internationally recognised education company that helps families of neurodivergent children thrive.
Over the next decade the company may expand into:
books · international keynote speaking · online education · digital products · membership communities · practical resources for parents and professionals · AI-powered education · coaching · innovative programs · programs that create genuine social impact
Zoe does not simply want to build a successful business. She wants to build something that genuinely changes lives.
How Zoe describes herself
She has ADHD and describes herself as a founder with many ideas.
She naturally:
sees opportunities
connects concepts
thinks strategically
creates new ideas
However, she loses energy when translating those ideas into:
operational systems
priorities
projects
workflows
documentation
automations
repeatable processes
What she is hiring
She described the person she is hiring as an operational translator.
She does not want someone who simply waits for instructions or completes repetitive tasks. She wants someone who naturally asks:
Why are we still doing this manually?
Could this be automated?
Is there a simpler way?
What would make this easier for the team?
She is looking for someone who enjoys building systems, improving workflows, organising information, solving operational problems, creating clarity from complexity, making businesses run more smoothly, challenging ideas respectfully, and recommending better approaches.
The engagement would initially likely be around one to two days per week. If the relationship works well, Zoe hopes it becomes a partnership measured in years rather than months.
Areas Zoe listed for help
the company's business operating system
scalable workflows
SOPs
CRM implementation and optimisation
AI integration throughout the business
workflow automations
team dashboards
project management systems
therapist workflows
client onboarding
internal documentation
knowledge management
course production systems
content production workflows
business reporting
continuous operational improvement
Technology Zoe mentioned
She mentioned possible familiarity with: ClickUp, GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Notion, Make, Zapier, n8n, ChatGPT, Claude, AI workflow design.
She clearly stated she is not looking for someone who is loyal to any particular software. She wants someone who recommends the right tool for the business and can confidently explain why another platform may be more appropriate.
Zoe's definition of success at six months
the business feels calmer
the team knows exactly what they are responsible for
ideas become projects
projects become systems
systems become habits
the company depends less on Zoe remembering everything
the business no longer lives entirely in her head
the business begins carrying itself
Treat this as one of the central outcomes of the roadmap.
Zoe's note on authenticity
Zoe said: "Please don't use AI to track it as we have AI trackers. We want to be working with those that have that real experience and are coming from a heart-led space."
Interpret this as a request for genuine experience and original thinking.
Do not attempt to manipulate AI detection systems. Do not deliberately add errors or awkward sentences.
The document should feel human because:
it is grounded in my actual experience
the recommendations are specific
the assumptions are transparent
the trade-offs are acknowledged
the priorities are realistic
the reasoning is explained
the writing reflects my natural voice
the plan includes practical limitations
the roadmap contains decisions I could defend personally
4. About me — for voice, not for claims
I am a Fractional COO with more than seven years of experience helping founder-led businesses turn ideas into clear plans, operational systems, workflows, accountable execution, team structures, documentation, reporting and repeatable processes.
My work is not limited to recommending platforms or writing SOPs. I normally help with:
operational diagnostics · business and operational planning · 30-60-90 day implementation roadmaps · project management systems · workflow design · SOPs · team accountability · KPIs and dashboards · hiring and onboarding · sales and client delivery systems · automations · CRM structure · quality control · capacity management · leadership rhythms · implementation and continuous improvement
I do not simply recommend systems and hand them over. I help implement them with the team, observe how they work in day-to-day operations, identify adoption issues, and improve them based on actual use.
I also have an implementation team that may support documentation, systems setup, project management, automation, dashboard development and execution where appropriate. This should not make the roadmap sound like I am selling a large agency package. It should simply show that implementation support is available if the workload requires it.
I typically begin with an operational diagnostic and a customised 30-60-90 Day Business and Operations Plan — an implementation blueprint rather than a strategy document that sits unused in a folder.
My personal connection to the mission
I am a mother of children on the autism spectrum. I understand first-hand how valuable the right therapy, education, resources, systems and family support can be. Helping build a company that supports neurodivergent children, their families and professionals is work I would genuinely be proud to contribute to.
Mention this naturally and briefly. Do not overuse it. Do not make it sound emotionally manipulative or as though personal experience replaces professional judgement. One or two sentences, in the closing.
5. What I already told Zoe
Everything in this section has already been said to her. The roadmap should be consistent with it and build on it — not contradict it, and not simply repeat it back.
My application opening
My application began with: "Building the machine."
I explained that the opportunity felt closely aligned with how I work, that I am a Fractional COO with over seven years of experience helping founder-led businesses turn ideas into clear plans, systems and accountable execution, and that I do not simply recommend tools or hand over SOPs — I build the operational structure, implement it with the team, and improve it based on what actually happens in the day-to-day business.
The case study I shared
I helped rebuild the sales and operations of a founder-led creator business that had strong revenue potential but inconsistent execution.

Problems included: scattered processes; difficulty measuring team performance; missed follow-ups; inconsistent execution; the founder being pulled into daily decisions.

I helped implement: clearer roles; sales workflows; SOPs; KPI dashboards; quality-control checkpoints; hiring systems; onboarding systems; structured management routines.

The business achieved 2.2 times monthly revenue growth through stronger systems and execution, not simply by hiring more people.

My reflection: I would involve the team earlier in the design stage. A good system can still fail when the people using it do not understand why it exists or do not feel ownership over it.

This principle should influence the Little Treasures roadmap. Reference the lesson in the roadmap, not the numbers — the numbers belong in the case study, which is attached separately.
The three areas I said I would investigate first
1. How ideas become projects
Where Zoe currently captures ideas · how ideas are prioritised · who owns the next step · how an idea becomes an approved project · where ideas or projects usually stall · how active projects are reviewed · how priorities are protected.

2. The full customer journey
Mapped across the clinical practice and the future education company: enquiry · onboarding · service delivery · communication · retention · courses · products · speaking · community.
The purpose is to identify gaps, handoffs, duplication, bottlenecks and opportunities for stronger systems.

3. Founder dependency
What only exists in Zoe's head · which decisions unnecessarily wait for her · what the team cannot move forward without her · what would stop if she stepped away for two weeks · what needs to be documented · what can be delegated · what can be standardised · what can later be automated · what should remain founder-led.
My technology position
I told Zoe I would not lock the business into a technology stack before understanding the actual workflows. I am not loyal to software. I am loyal to what makes the business easier to manage and easier for the team to use.

My preliminary direction included: ClickUp for execution, projects, launches, ownership and dashboards · HubSpot or GoHighLevel for CRM and customer journeys · Kajabi or similar for courses and digital products · Circle if membership and community become core offers · a structured knowledge base for SOPs, training and IP · Make, Zapier or n8n for integrations and automations · ChatGPT or Claude for approved AI workflows · privacy, quality-control and human-review standards for AI.

My main principle: the business should have one clear source of truth rather than a collection of disconnected platforms the team has to update manually.

These were preliminary possibilities only. Do not treat these platforms as final recommendations in the roadmap. See Section 9 for how to handle technology.
My example of challenging a client
One client wanted to add more responsibilities without adjusting the existing scope, priorities, capacity or resources. Instead of immediately agreeing and allowing the quality of the work to suffer, I explained the trade-offs and presented three options: reprioritise existing work, phase the new initiative, or add the appropriate capacity.

The client understood because I did not simply reject the idea — I explained what the additional work would require and what would be affected.

My lesson: I would raise capacity risks earlier and support the discussion with stronger performance and capacity data.

My operating belief: a good operations partner should not agree with everything. Sometimes my responsibility is to say, "Yes, we can do that, but here is what it will take."

This principle is important because Zoe has many ideas and a broad long-term vision. The roadmap should show that not every opportunity should become an immediate active project.
My two-year vision for the role
After working together successfully for two years, I would hope:
Zoe is no longer carrying the business in her head
her ideas are captured, assessed and turned into clear projects
the team knows what they own
the team understands what they can decide
the team knows when Zoe genuinely needs to be involved
the clinical practice runs consistently
the education company has the systems to support courses, books, digital products, speaking, partnerships and community
the business grows without becoming heavier or more chaotic
Zoe has more time for the work only she can do
she can focus more on creating, teaching, speaking and building relationships
6. My core operational principles — use these throughout
1. Diagnose before prescribing. I would not change platforms or rebuild systems without understanding the business. Before major decisions I would assess: the current business model, current priorities, current workflows, existing technology, team structure, team capacity, pain points, client experience, clinical workflows, founder dependency, data and reporting, privacy requirements, budget, adoption risks.
2. Stabilise before scaling. The current clinical practice is the operational foundation. The business should not attempt to launch every future idea at once. Before aggressively expanding into books, courses, digital products, speaking, membership, coaching or AI-powered education, the roadmap should create the operational foundation that allows growth without creating unnecessary chaos.
3. Prioritise before executing. Zoe has many ideas. There should be a clear system for capturing ideas, evaluating them, identifying strategic fit, estimating effort, understanding capacity, deciding what happens now and what happens later, assigning ownership, defining expected outcomes, and stopping or pausing low-priority initiatives.
4. Process before automation. Do not automate a process before it is understood. The sequence is: investigate → map → simplify → remove unnecessary steps → standardise → assign ownership → document → test → train → automate where appropriate → measure → improve.
5. Adoption is more important than documentation. A system is not complete simply because an SOP exists. Implementation includes team involvement, clear reasoning, training, recorded walkthroughs, feedback, testing, adjustment, adoption monitoring, accountability, reinforcement and review cycles.
6. One clear source of truth. The team should know where to find priorities, projects, tasks, deadlines, responsibilities, decisions, SOPs, training materials, client information, content assets, reports and performance data. Avoid duplicate manual updating across several platforms.
7. Technology must support the workflow. Software should not define the strategy. Each technology recommendation should answer: what problem it solves, why the current process is insufficient, why the platform fits the team, what must be validated first, who owns the platform, how it will be maintained, how duplicate work will be prevented, how data moves between platforms, and what happens when the system fails.
8. Preserve human-led care. AI and automation may support administration, internal drafting, knowledge retrieval, content support, task creation, reporting, repetitive communication and workflow routing. AI must not replace clinical judgement, therapist decision-making, professional review, sensitive family communication, consent, safeguarding, or appropriate human oversight.
9. Protect sensitive information. Because Little Treasures works with children, families and healthcare-related information, all AI, CRM, automation and data recommendations must consider privacy, consent, user access, data security, information storage, clinical boundaries, human review, confidentiality, and applicable Australian legal and professional requirements. Do not make definitive legal claims. State that recommendations would need to be validated with the appropriate privacy, legal, clinical, cybersecurity or compliance professional.
10. Build for continuity. The systems must not become dependent on me. Every major process should include an owner, a backup owner, an SOP, a process map where useful, a recorded walkthrough, access documentation, system administration instructions, maintenance requirements, review frequency, change history, handover notes and escalation procedures.
7. Preliminary six-month roadmap direction
This is my working hypothesis. Challenge it, simplify it, or adjust it where necessary. Do not automatically include every item — the point is strong prioritisation, not a long list of everything possible.
Month 1 — Discovery, visibility and prioritisation
Understand the business before making major system or technology decisions.

Possible activities: detailed founder interview · review of Zoe's short- and long-term goals · identification of the next 12-month priorities · team and stakeholder interviews · team responsibility review · team capacity review · current workflow audit · current systems and subscription audit · clinical client journey mapping · therapist workflow mapping · administrative workflow mapping · founder-dependency assessment · current project and idea inventory · review of existing documentation · review of reporting and metrics · review of current communication channels · review of privacy, access and data risks · identification of immediate operational issues · prioritisation of the six-month implementation backlog

Possible deliverables: Current-State Operational Assessment · Founder-Dependency Map · Workflow and Systems Map · Team Responsibility and Capacity Map · Technology and Subscription Audit · Current Client Journey Map · Risk and Opportunity Register · Prioritised Operational Backlog · Baseline KPI Scorecard · Confirmed Six-Month Implementation Scope

Reason: the roadmap cannot responsibly prescribe a final operating model without understanding the current business.
Success before moving forward: the most important operational issues have been identified · Zoe and the team agree on the top priorities · current workflows and systems are visible · major assumptions have been validated or corrected · the six-month scope is clear · the team understands what will change first and why
Month 2 — Business operating system and accountability
Create the structure that turns ideas and priorities into owned execution.

Possible activities: configure or improve the central project management platform · create the idea-capture process · create the idea-evaluation process · create the project-intake process · define project stages · define ownership · clarify decision rights · define escalation rules · create recurring planning and review rhythms · create team dashboards · create project dashboards · establish documentation standards · design the knowledge-base structure · introduce the new operating rhythm · train the team

Possible deliverables: Business Operating System · Idea-to-Initiative Workflow · Idea Evaluation Scorecard · Project Intake Form · Project Brief Template · Project Stage Definitions · Responsibility Matrix · Decision and Escalation Matrix · Weekly Operating Rhythm · Leadership Dashboard · Project Dashboard · Knowledge-Base Architecture · Documentation Standards · Team Training Materials · Recorded Platform Walkthroughs

Reason: before improving individual workflows, the business needs a reliable way to manage priorities, ownership, projects, decisions and information.

Success before moving forward: ideas are captured in one location · active initiatives are visible · every project has a clear owner · the team understands where work is managed · Zoe can see what is moving, blocked, delayed or waiting for her · recurring operational meetings use consistent information · the team has started using the operating system consistently
Month 3 — Core clinical and administrative workflows
Focus on the highest-impact workflows inside the current clinical practice.
Do not assume every workflow will be rebuilt. Discovery should determine which two or three workflows create the most delay, rework, confusion, founder dependency, administrative burden or client frustration.

Possible workflow areas: enquiry management · intake · client onboarding · therapist assignment · internal handoffs · scheduling-related coordination · client or parent communication · document collection · service delivery support · therapist administration · clinical-to-administrative handoffs · escalation · quality control · discharge or offboarding · follow-up communication

Possible deliverables: Prioritised Client Journey Map · Improved Enquiry Workflow · Improved Intake Workflow · Client Onboarding Checklist · Therapist Handoff Process · Communication Templates · Escalation Procedures · Quality-Control Checkpoints · Exception-Handling Procedures · Selected Core SOPs · Process Maps · Team Training · Workflow Testing Log · Adoption and Feedback Log

Reason: the clinical practice is the current foundation of the company. Improving the highest-impact workflows can reduce pressure on Zoe and the team while improving consistency for families.

Success before moving forward: ownership is clear · handoffs are documented · avoidable steps are removed · the selected workflows have been tested · the team has been trained · recurring issues are tracked · the processes no longer depend on one person remembering every step
Month 4 — CRM, reporting and responsible automation
Focus on information flow, visibility, and automation of stable processes. Do not finalise a CRM or automation platform before discovery.

Possible activities: define CRM requirements · evaluate existing tools · select or optimise the appropriate CRM · define lifecycle and pipeline stages · define data-entry requirements · clarify system ownership · reduce duplicate data entry · create approved integrations · automate repetitive and low-risk administrative tasks · create human-review checkpoints · create failure notifications · build operational dashboards · define reporting responsibilities · train the team · document system maintenance

Possible deliverables: CRM Requirements Document · CRM Recommendation or Configuration Plan · Client Lifecycle Definitions · Pipeline Stage Definitions · Data Standards · System Ownership Matrix · Priority Automations · Automation Register · Automation Process Maps · Error and Exception Procedures · Human-Review Checkpoints · Operational Dashboard · KPI Definitions · Reporting Calendar · System Administration Guides · Team Training Materials

Possible early automation examples: enquiry routing · internal task creation · reminders · follow-up alerts · status updates · handoff notifications · project creation · document-request reminders · reporting updates
Do not recommend automating sensitive clinical communication or decision-making without appropriate review.

Reason: automation should follow process clarification and team adoption.
Success before moving forward: the required data is clearly defined · system ownership is assigned · selected workflows are stable · priority integrations work reliably · failure points are documented · team members understand how to use the CRM · reporting no longer depends entirely on manual updates · automations reduce work without creating hidden risks
Month 5 — Education and content operating foundation
Prepare the operational foundation for the education-company vision.
The goal is not to launch books, courses, membership, speaking, coaching, digital products and AI education all at once. The goal is a repeatable process for deciding which idea moves forward and how it will be produced.

Possible activities: capture Zoe's current education and content ideas · organise existing intellectual property · identify existing content and resources · create an opportunity-evaluation framework · assess strategic fit · assess audience need · assess required capacity · assess possible revenue or impact · assess delivery complexity · select one priority pilot initiative · create a content or education production workflow · define review and approval stages · create asset-management standards · define AI-assisted content boundaries · create a launch-readiness process · assign ownership

Possible deliverables: Education Opportunity Inventory · Idea Evaluation Framework · Priority Scorecard · Content and Intellectual Property Library · Education Product Development Workflow · Content Production Workflow · Review and Approval Workflow · AI Usage and Human-Review Guidelines · Asset Naming and Storage Standards · Launch Readiness Checklist · Pilot Initiative Project Plan · Responsibility Matrix for the Pilot
Possible pilot initiatives — one only: a practical parent resource · a professional resource · a small digital product · a workshop · an educational webinar · a short online program · a content series
Do not choose the pilot without evidence from discovery.
Reason: the business should create a reliable way to move from ideas to validated education initiatives without overwhelming the clinical practice.

Success before moving forward: ideas are assessed consistently · one initiative has been selected based on clear criteria · ownership and production stages are defined · existing IP is organised · content review standards are clear · the team understands what should be developed now and what remains in the future backlog
Month 6 — Optimisation, adoption, continuity and next-stage planning
Ensure the systems are being used, improve what is not working, and make the operating model resilient.
Possible activities: review adoption · review workflow performance · interview Zoe and team members · identify recurring friction · improve dashboards · complete documentation gaps · confirm system owners · confirm backup owners · create system administration guides · organise access records · cross-train team members · test whether another person can follow the key processes · test continuity if I am unavailable · consolidate the operations handbook · create the next six-to-twelve-month roadmap

Possible deliverables: Six-Month Operational Review · Adoption and Compliance Review · Workflow Improvement Log · Updated SOP Library · Operations Handbook · System Ownership Register · Access and Permission Register · Automation Register · Change Log · Business Continuity Plan · Cross-Training Records · Operations Handover Pack · Training Library · Next Six-to-Twelve-Month Roadmap

Reason: a system is not sustainable until ownership, training, adoption, maintenance and handover are established.
Success by the end of six months: the team uses the agreed operating system · key workflows have clear owners · selected processes are documented and tested · Zoe has better visibility · fewer routine decisions wait for Zoe · the business has an organised knowledge base · selected automations are documented and monitored · another qualified Operations Manager could understand the current systems · the next phase of the education-company roadmap is clear
8. Sustainability requirements
The roadmap must clearly explain how I would prevent the company from becoming dependent on me.

By the end of six months, the business should have a continuity structure that may include:
central operations handbook · organised SOP library · process maps · responsibility matrix · decision matrix · escalation matrix · system ownership register · backup owner register · access and permission register · automation register · integration map · system administration guides · data definitions · reporting definitions · recurring reporting calendar · meeting rhythm documentation · project templates · training materials · recorded walkthroughs · change log · decision log · known-issues register · vendor and subscription register · handover checklist · business continuity plan · cross-training records · new Operations Manager onboarding guide

Do not include all of these merely to create a long list. Select the continuity assets that are most useful and realistic. Explain that documentation should be updated as processes change.

The section must also explain how another Operations Manager could step in and continue successfully, covering documentation, ownership, training, access, maintenance, continuity, handover and cross-training. (Ideally, we can always mention that GIM can handle this. Hahaha! Wag overthinker mimakerls)
9. Technology handling — platform-neutral
Zoe explicitly said she is not looking for someone loyal to any particular software.
Do not name a recommended platform stack in the client-facing roadmap. No tool comparison table.
The tools Zoe listed are ones she is familiar with, not necessarily ones the business runs on. Do not treat that list as an inventory of current systems.
Refer to systems by function, not brand: "the central project and priority system", "the practice management system", "the automation layer".
Do state the criteria a platform decision would be made against — see Principle 7.
The platform decision is explicitly one of the decisions held until discovery is complete.
AI and automation language
Do not position AI as the centre of the strategy, despite the role title. AI is one possible operational tool.
The roadmap should make clear that: AI should have a defined use case · sensitive information should be protected · human review should remain · clinical judgement should not be automated · staff should understand when AI can and cannot be used · outputs should be reviewed · approved tools should be documented · AI processes should have ownership · privacy requirements should be validated · automation should not be added simply because it is possible.
10. Assumptions that must be labelled
The roadmap may assume the following — but each must be visibly labelled as an assumption, never presented as fact. For each major assumption, explain what could change if it is incorrect.
the clinical practice is currently operating
the clinical practice will remain the immediate foundation of the company
the education-company vision is still developing
not every planned offer currently exists
Zoe currently holds important information, decisions or ideas in her head
founder dependency is a meaningful issue
existing systems may be fragmented
existing documentation may be incomplete
the team will need training and change-management support
current technology has not yet been fully assessed
current workflows have not yet been fully mapped
data and performance baselines may be limited
access to relevant systems and team members will be provided
implementation time is limited to approximately one to two days per week
some technical work may require implementation support
sensitive client or clinical information must be protected
Australian privacy, legal and clinical requirements must be validated
the education work in the first six months will likely be foundational or pilot-based
the roadmap will need to be adjusted after discovery
Select the highest-impact six to eight for the client-facing table. The rest can sit in the appendix.
11. Scope reality — be honest
The initial role is approximately one to two days per week. The plan must be realistic at that level of involvement. Do not create a roadmap that assumes full-time work. Do not promise to completely rebuild every area of the business in six months.
Clearly distinguish work that would be: fully implemented · designed · documented · piloted · partially implemented · dependent on the team · dependent on specialist support · deferred to a later phase.
Reasonably achievable in six months at 1–2 days per week
operational discovery · priority mapping · business operating system design and implementation · idea-to-project workflow · accountability structure · knowledge-base structure · selected workflow improvements · selected SOPs · selected dashboards · CRM requirements and preliminary implementation · selected low-risk automations · education-production foundation · one pilot initiative plan · continuity and handover documentation
Not realistic in the same window
rebuild every clinical workflow · migrate every system · implement a complete CRM transformation · launch multiple education products · create a full membership community · produce a complete online course library · establish an international speaking business · create multiple books · fully automate the business · build advanced custom AI platforms · complete every SOP · build every dashboard · create every future revenue stream
Where necessary, explain that implementation capacity may need to increase if Zoe wants more initiatives completed within the same six-month period.
The final roadmap should show strong prioritisation. Do not make a long list of everything that could possibly be done.
12. Discovery information I would need
This is the full set of what I would investigate in the first few weeks. Only the most important areas go in the client-facing roadmap — the rest goes in the appendix.
Business strategy
What are Zoe's top three priorities for the next 12 months? · Which parts of the ten-year vision are already active? · Which ideas have already been validated? · Which opportunities are still conceptual? · What does Zoe want to remain personally responsible for? · What does she want to stop owning? · What should the business deliberately not build yet? · What outcomes matter most after six months?
Current business model
What services does the clinical practice currently provide? · What are the current revenue streams? · What is the current client volume? · What is the current demand? · Are there waitlists? · Which services create the strongest demand? · Which services create the greatest operational pressure? · What education, training or digital offers already exist? · What partnerships already exist? · What intellectual property already exists?
Note: financial information does not need to appear in the final roadmap. The point is to show what should be investigated.
Team
Who is currently on the team? · What are their roles? · Who manages daily operations? · Who owns administration? · Who supports therapists? · Who supports content or education? · What responsibilities are unclear? · Where is work duplicated? · What decisions wait for Zoe? · What is the current team capacity? · What is the team's technology capability? · Who should be involved in designing new workflows? · Where is cross-training currently missing?
Clinical operations
What is the current journey from enquiry to service completion? · How are enquiries captured? · How are clients onboarded? · How are therapists assigned? · How are documents collected? · How is communication managed? · Which processes create delays? · Which information is entered repeatedly? · Which workflows depend on manual reminders? · Which decisions require Zoe? · What creates frustration for therapists? · What creates frustration for families? · What quality controls currently exist? · What escalation procedures exist? · How is discharge or offboarding managed?
Technology
What platforms are currently used? · Which platforms are working? · Which are not being used consistently? · Where is data duplicated? · What is currently the source of truth? · What integrations exist? · Which subscriptions are unnecessary? · Who owns each platform? · Who has administrator access? · What backups exist? · What reporting is currently available? · What privacy and security requirements apply? · Where is sensitive information stored? · What software budget is available?
Projects and ideas
Where does Zoe currently store ideas? · How are ideas evaluated? · How are projects approved? · How are projects prioritised? · How are projects assigned? · How does Zoe review progress? · How many active projects currently exist? · Which projects are stalled? · Which ideas should remain in a future backlog? · What causes new initiatives to lose momentum?
Education company
Which audience should the company serve first — parents, therapists, schools, clinics, professionals, international audiences? · What audience already exists? · What existing content has performed well? · What questions do families repeatedly ask? · What resources do professionals repeatedly need? · What products or programs are already being considered? · What is the strongest possible pilot? · What level of clinical review is required? · Who will support research, writing, production, approval, launch and customer support?
Reporting
What numbers does Zoe currently review? · What information does she wish she had? · What should leadership see weekly? · What should the team see? · What should be reviewed monthly? · How is client experience measured? · How is team capacity measured? · How is operational performance measured? · What baseline information is available?
13. Hard rules — do not break these
Do not invent anything. Specifically, do not invent or imply:
experience I have not had
team members, team size or roles at Little Treasures
revenue, client numbers, waitlists, pricing or any figure
current workflows, current software or current documentation
operational problems Zoe has not confirmed
measurable outcomes for Little Treasures
market statistics
quotes from Zoe beyond what is in this brief
Where information is missing, label it as an assumption, a discovery item, a dependency or a preliminary recommendation.
Do not present assumptions as facts. Do not claim any six-month outcome is guaranteed.
Do not make recommendations I would struggle to explain in an interview. If you cannot articulate the reasoning in one sentence, cut it.
Do not write a generic AI-style operations plan. Do not make it sound overly polished, exaggerated or impersonal.


Do not write Write instead
A named diagnostic framework or methodology of mine Describe what the diagnostic covers and produces, in plain language
Named past clients, industries or projects One line noting a case study is included separately
The 2.2x figure or any past performance number Reference the  lesson  — involving the team earlier in design
Claims about clinical, allied health or NDIS experience Frame clinical workflow observations as areas to investigate
My implementation team's size, cost or capacity One neutral sentence: additional implementation support is available if more is to be delivered in the same window
Any rate, retainer or pricing Omit entirely — no investment section, no next-steps sales sequence
Confident statements about Australian privacy or professional obligations State these would be validated with the appropriate privacy, legal, clinical, cybersecurity or compliance adviser14. What you are producing
Deliverable 1 — The roadmap (client-facing)
Length: 4–6 pages. Hard constraint from Zoe. Closer to 5 than 6. She does not want every possible idea included — she wants the thinking distilled into a clear, structured, actionable plan.
It should make it easy to understand: the actions I would take · the order I would take them in · why that sequence matters · the milestones I would achieve · the deliverables that would exist · how success would be evaluated.
Deliver in markdown so I can edit quickly.
Deliverable 2 — Supporting appendix (internal, for me only)
Not submitted to Zoe. Two parts:
Discovery question set — the full set of questions from Section 12 above, expanded into questions I could work through on a call, grouped and ordered by area. Aim for 40–60.
Deferred-item backlog — everything deliberately excluded from the six months (Section 11), each with a one-line note on what would need to be true for it to start. Deferral must look like a decision, not an omission.
2–4 pages. Flexible.
15. Required structure for the roadmap
Zoe asked for four things: Six-Month Vision · Roadmap · Sustainability · Discovery. All four must be visibly and directly answered.

Title page Little Treasures Company · Six-Month Operational Roadmap · Prepared by Divine Grace Origines, Fractional COO Optional subtitle: Building the operational foundation for a calmer, more scalable, and less founder-dependent business.

1. Executive overview — ~0.5 page My understanding of Zoe's vision · the operational goal of the first six months · the importance of stabilising the core before scaling · the importance of translating ideas into prioritised execution · the fact that the roadmap is preliminary and will be refined after discovery. Keep concise. Exclude: restating the job post, selling, listing tools.

2. Six-month vision — ~0.75 page Describe exactly what should exist after six months. Focus on the operating reality rather than a list of tools. May include: one central operating system · clear priorities · visible projects · clear ownership · documented decision rights · selected clinical and administrative workflows · core SOPs · knowledge management · dashboards · selected CRM and automation foundations · an education opportunity framework · a pilot education project · continuity and handover systems.

3. Six-month roadmap — ~1.5–2 pages. The core of the document. A concise table, one row per month or phase. Columns: Phase · Focus · Why it happens now · Key actions · Deliverables · Success before moving forward. Keep it readable. Do not make every cell excessively long, and keep cell depth consistent. Add two or three sentences beneath the table explaining the sequencing logic — process before automation, stabilise before scale. Exclude: week-by-week breakdowns, sub-tables.

4. Scope and honesty — ~0.5 page Four short grouped lists: fully implemented · designed and piloted · dependent on Zoe and the team · deliberately deferred. Note that implementation capacity may need to increase for more to be completed in the same window. Tone: command of the work, not apology.

5. Sustainability and continuity — ~0.75 page How the systems would be designed so another Operations Manager could continue successfully. Cover documentation · ownership · training · access · maintenance · continuity · handover · cross-training. Be selective about which continuity assets you name.

6. Discovery and assumptions — ~0.75 page Two concise parts: first-weeks discovery priorities (the three investigation areas from Section 5), then key assumptions and dependencies as a small table with a "what changes if it is wrong" column — six to eight rows only. Then two or three decisions explicitly held until discovery is complete, with reasons. Exclude: the full question list. That is the appendix.

7. Closing outcome — ~0.25 page A concise explanation of what Zoe and the team should experience after six months: greater calm · clearer ownership · better visibility · reduced founder dependency · better execution · stronger clinical foundations · a disciplined path toward the education-company vision.
